source.authors: van der Kooi CJ, Stavenga DG, Arikawa K, Belušič G, Kelber A
source.title: Evolution of insect color vision: from spectral sensitivity to visual ecology

quote: Hymenoptera and Lepidoptera have three ommatidial types, with two blue receptors, two UV receptors, or one blue and one UV receptor (5, 103, 143). In Hymenoptera, six receptors are green sensitive
note: nine receptors per ommatidium in bees (same section); the three ommatidial types are randomly arranged with dorsoventral gradients in frequency

method: review statement: facet lens chitin absorbs far UV

source.authors: van der Kooi CJ, Stavenga DG, Arikawa K, Belušič G, Kelber A

quote: Consequently, the spectral sensitivity of insect photoreceptors becomes minor near 300 nm
note: lower limit only; the facet lens chitin absorbs the far UV
review reporting Srinivasan MV, Lehrer M 1988, J Comp Physiol A 162:159-172; a person resolves about 60 cycles/degree, so 0.26 is about 1/230 of a person
method: behavioural: trained discrimination of vertical and horizontal gratings at different distances (Srinivasan and Lehrer 1988)

source.authors: Land MF
source.title: Visual acuity in insects

quote: Drone bees have a similar anterodorsal acute zone, where the density of ommatidial axes is three to four times greater than in the female eye (Figure 7c). They use this region when chasing the queen

note: single-object threshold, set by a brief 6% dimming of sky light in one rhabdom (same page)
value: pursues targets subtending 0.32 degrees, smaller than the 1.2 degree acceptance angle
method: behavioural: minimum target that evokes pursuit (Vallet and Coles 1991)

source.authors: Land MF
source.title: Visual acuity in insects

quote: The minimum target size that a drone will pursue subtends 0.32◦, which is much smaller than the ommatidial acceptance angle of 1.2◦ (77).

note: the review says the same pattern is documented in worker honey bees, with smaller horizontal and larger vertical variation than in butterflies; the horizontal extreme lies about 40 degrees from the midline
value: frontal acute zone and an equatorial band of finer vertical sampling (forward flight pattern)
method: anatomical maps of interommatidial angles (Land 1989; Seidl 1982)

source.authors: Land MF
source.title: Visual acuity in insects

quote: This results in a frontal acute zone and a band around the equator with enhanced vertical, but not horizontal, acuity (38). This pattern was first noticed in bees and butterflies

note: integration times in most insects are 5-50 ms (same page); insects routinely turn at hundreds of degrees per second
value: motion blur above about 50 degrees per second for a 1 degree acceptance angle and 20 ms integration time
method: optical theory (Snyder 1979) with typical insect values

source.authors: Land MF
source.title: Visual acuity in insects

quote: Thus if an insect has 1ρ = 1◦ and 1t = 20 ms, then blur will occur at angular velocities greater than 50◦ s−1.

note: general statement; nocturnal bees and hornets are exceptions treated elsewhere in the log
value: resolution compromised below room light; diurnal insects do not fly dimmer than this
method: photon-catch calculation for a diurnal apposition eye (D 25 µm, d 2 µm, f 60 µm)

source.authors: Land MF
source.title: Visual acuity in insects

quote: It is then clear that resolution will be always compromised in illumination conditions dimmer than roomlight. Diurnal insects do not fly in light levels lower than this.
